clauses.reason: Whole order (single operative paragraph, offsets 0-647 of the held text jobs/app-executive-orders/output/texts/executive-order-8584-exemption-frank-burke-from-compulsory-retirement-for-age.txt): signed November 7, 1940. The recital finds that the public interest requires that the employee be further exempted from compulsory retirement for age for a period of one year, and the operative sentence, under section 204 of the act of June 30, 1932 (47 Stat. 382, 404), further exempts Frank Burke from compulsory retirement for age for a period of one year ending December 31, 1941. That exemption is the order's only command and it carries its own fixed term. The recital names the earlier exemption Executive Order No. 8302 of December 12, 1939; those are earlier instruments, not events on this order. First end: the order's own stated end, December 31, 1941 (operative sentence: "for a period of one year ending December 31, 1941."). The stated date is recorded inclusive (the exemption runs through the end of December 31, 1941); the exclusive reading, under which it ends when December 31, 1941 begins, is the alternative. The date is the end of the stated term, not a record of separation or death; no such record is held. Later event, not an end: Executive Order 9002, signed December 29, 1941, further exempts the same person; its recital names this order ("Executive Orders No. 8302 of December 12, 1939, and No. 8584 of November 7, 1940") and its operative sentence runs "ending December 31, 1942". Like this order it has no effective-date wording, so I read it as effective on signing.

savings.reason: The exemption let Frank Burke remain in service past the retirement age that would otherwise have required automatic separation; service rendered while the exemption ran is an accrued effect that remains after the stated end date. The order says nothing about any status, right or duty after December 31, 1941, so no independent continuing command or residual obligation of this order survives its stated term. Later service under the further exemption came from a separate order, not from this one.
